_note: Second reading of AI reader 120's anchors (the day after: nicotine, cocaine, ADHD stimulants; seven local PDFs).

tasks.locator: Abstract; Method › Study selection and synthesis, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Data extraction and synthesis, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: A single-author review of studies from 1990 to 2004: more than 3,500 citations, 792 abstracts read, 290 articles read and 120 cited; inclusion required published prospective studies of cigarettes with more than 18 hours of abstinence; the author chose which results to include on his subjective opinion of rigor, consistency and size, and states that data collection and interpretation rested solely on his judgments.

tasks.locator: Results › Description of abstinence effects, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1
tasks.extracted: Conclusions rest mainly on 15 comprehensive prospective studies of 11 to 178 people: all but one had pre-quit values, 9 used control arms of trials, and only 2 had control groups, 2 generalizable samples, 3 more than 90 participants and 5 low attrition; no meta-analysis was done because of methodological heterogeneity.

tasks.locator: Results › Anger/irritability/frustration, 2nd paragraph; Anxiety, 2nd paragraph; Depression, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Anger peaks within the first week and lasts 2 weeks (7 studies), 3 weeks (1) or 4 weeks or more (2); anxiety rose in the first 1 to 3 days and lasted about 2 weeks in most studies, though one study of well-validated abstainers found a fall; low mood rose in 6 core studies but not in 2 (a third found a fall), peaking at 1, 2 or 3 weeks and still raised at 30 days in two, and the author calls this evidence surprisingly mixed.

tasks.locator: Results › Difficulty concentrating, 2nd paragraph (p. 319); Impatience, 2nd paragraph (p. 320); Insomnia (pp. 320-321); Restlessness, 2nd paragraph (p. 322)
tasks.extracted: Difficulty concentrating peaked in the first few days and lasted from a week or less to 4 weeks or more; impatience rose for 3 to 4 weeks or more in all 3 newer studies; sleep fragmentation (waking at night) increased consistently in sleep-EEG and clinical studies lasting 5 to 14 days, with more recall of vivid dreams; restlessness peaked on days 1 to 3 and lasted 2 to 4 weeks.

tasks.locator: Results › Drowsiness/decreased alertness or arousal, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Fatigue (p. 320); Physical symptoms, 1st to 4th paragraphs (pp. 321-322)
tasks.extracted: Alertness fell in 2, rose in 2 and did not change in 3 core studies; fatigue did not change in 3 of 4 studies; all studies were negative for headaches, sweating, a racing heart, tremor and skin rash; dizziness rose transiently in two studies but not in a third; constipation, cough and mouth ulcers were each found in one study.

tasks.locator: Results › Time course, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Total withdrawal scores were back at or very near pre-quit levels after about 2 weeks and by 3 to 4 weeks, so the author states that the syndrome lasts 2 to 4 weeks; onset could not be determined; in two studies 38% and 61% of people did not follow the average course (symptoms rose again about 3 weeks after quitting, or did not fall); one study suggests retrospective reports overestimate duration; prolonged withdrawal of 6 months or more does not appear to occur, except possibly for craving and hunger.

tasks.locator: Methods › Search strategy; Inclusion/exclusion criteria
tasks.extracted: Searches ended on 31 May 2011 and were limited to English-language papers from 2004 onwards; eligible trials were randomized crossover or parallel trials with at least 2 hours of abstinence before baseline; people in cessation programmes or using NRT were excluded.

tasks.locator: Results › Study characteristics and quality assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1
tasks.extracted: 19 randomized trials (7 parallel, 12 crossover; 14 published, the rest theses) with 10 to 84 participants each; bouts of 5 to 40 minutes, mostly moderate walking or cycling, against passive controls; craving rated immediately before and after the bout, or 5 minutes after it in three studies.

tasks.locator: Results › All eligible studies › Two-stage random-effects meta-analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 30); Tables 2 and 3 (p. 32)
tasks.extracted: Strength of desire −1.91 (95% CI −2.59 to −1.22), 15 studies, 797 observations, I² 94.2%; desire to smoke −2.03 (−2.60 to −1.46), 17 studies, 837 observations, I² 92.0%.

tasks.locator: Results › One-stage individual participant data meta-analysis; Parallel arm studies; Studies investigating physical activity of moderate intensity; Tables 2 and 3
tasks.extracted: One-stage model −1.89 (−2.52 to −1.26) and −2.03 (−2.54 to −1.51), with 95% mid-ranges of −3.56 to −0.22 and −3.45 to −0.62; parallel trials only −1.78 and −2.27; moderate intensity only −2.20 and −2.14.

tasks.locator: Figures 2 and 3 (pp. 33-34); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 34) and last paragraph (p. 35)
tasks.extracted: Every study favoured exercise, from −0.22 to −4.54 points for strength of desire; the three isometric-exercise studies had the smallest effects, with intervals including zero in two of them for strength of desire (−0.55 and −0.22), and the largest effect came from the study with the highest baseline craving.

tasks.locator: Abstract (p. 26); Methods › Data analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 28); Results › One-stage individual participant data meta-analysis (p. 32)
tasks.extracted: The abstract reports the pooled results as standardized mean differences, but the methods derive each effect as the difference between groups in post-intervention ratings adjusted for baseline, and the one-stage model reports a mean difference.

tasks.locator: Results › Literature search (p. 28); Study characteristics and quality assessment, 4th paragraph (p. 30); Declarations of interest (p. 35)
tasks.extracted: Titles were screened by the first author alone; quality was reported only as randomization (one study allocated by recruitment order); the review was paid for from internal institutional funds with no industry links; editors' count from the reference list: 17 of the 19 included trials list at least one of the review's authors.

tasks.locator: Abstract; Materials and methods › Search strategy; Selection and characterisation of studies; Results, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Of 27 studies reporting effects of oral nicotine on at least one withdrawal symptom, 12 met the criteria (published placebo-controlled randomized trials, product started within 24 hours of stopping, symptoms assessed over at least 24 hours in the usual environment, biochemical verification): 8 gum, 3 inhaler, 1 sublingual tablet and no lozenge; good data existed only for the first week.

tasks.locator: Table 3, bottom row and n column (read on the rendered, rotated page)
tasks.extracted: Fractions of trials finding a significant effect in the first week: irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2, hunger 2/5, total withdrawal 6/7, craving 7/11; trials had 15 to 240 participants.

tasks.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 117); Table 3, craving column (p. 121)
tasks.extracted: Craving was reduced in all three inhaler trials and the single tablet trial but in only 3 of 7 gum trials.

tasks.locator: Table 2, Design and Comments rows
tasks.extracted: Lapsers were kept in the analyses in five trials (Hughes et al., 1984, 1989, 1990 and 1991; Gross & Stitzer, 1989); more people dropped out of the placebo group in three trials; West et al. (1984) used low-nicotine gum rather than placebo as the comparator.

tasks.locator: Results, 3rd and 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors state that in most trials people were analysed even if only partially abstinent, and that the number of studies was too small for any pattern to show unless very marked; no differences were seen by date, size, inclusion of lapsers, use of baselines or product use.

tasks.locator: Table 3, footnote b; Acknowledgements
tasks.extracted: Blanks in Table 3 mean that the effect was not tested or not reported; the review was funded by SmithKline Beecham.

tasks.locator: Subjects and Methods › Sample (p. 108); Procedures › Ratings and Raters (p. 109); Table 1 (p. 108)
tasks.extracted: Thirty consecutive self-referred outpatients (mean age 28.6, 73% men; 43% injected, 37% intranasal, 20% smoked) with heavy weekly use; raters were the treating therapists and were not blind to reports of cocaine use; abstinence was corroborated by urinalysis and by significant others.

tasks.locator: Clinical Findings › Abstinence Phenomenon, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Phase 1: Crash, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The course is described for the 14 people without other diagnoses, from observation and from accounts of earlier attempts to stop; when supplies ran out, low mood mounted within 15 to 30 minutes of the last dose with intense craving; the crash then brought low mood, loss of pleasure, insomnia, irritability, anxiety and confusion, ending one to 40 hours after use stopped, followed by eight to 50 hours of heavy sleep with waking and overeating; passing suicidal ideation (43% of the subsample) and paranoia (36%) were limited to this phase.

tasks.locator: Figure and legend (p. 110); Phase 1: Crash, 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 111)
tasks.extracted: Craving was absent in the late crash and during heavy sleep; over 80% used alcohol or opioids at least once to sleep; five people whose ordered cocaine arrived 2 to 5 hours after their last dose did not use it; eight people described a crash of at most 3 days and the rest up to 6 days, while the figure gives 9 hours to 4 days.

tasks.locator: Clinical Findings › Abstinence Symptoms and Diagnosis, 1st paragraph; Comment, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: All people with other diagnoses and four others were treated with medication, so the later phases were not observed without it in most; the authors call the findings preliminary, limited by small numbers and the lack of structured instruments or blind observation; editors' count: 20 of the 30 took medication.

tasks.locator: Results › Subject Characteristics, 3rd paragraph; Outcome › Mood Scores and Craving for Cocaine (p. 864); Figure 2 and Table 2 (p. 865)
tasks.extracted: In a controlled residential study, all men had used cocaine within 48 hours before admission; mood distress and craving were highest on admission day and fell over the 28 days (craving F = 17.270, P<.01); sleep reports did not differ from controls except more difficulty falling asleep.

tasks.locator: Subjects and Methods › Subjects, 8th and 9th paragraphs (p. 862); Research Procedures, 3rd paragraph (p. 863); Table 1 (p. 863)
tasks.extracted: Of thirty men with cocaine dependence who made appointments, sixteen came, fourteen were admitted and 12 completed; ten controls completed; measures were taken on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14, 18, 21, 25 and 28 between 9 AM and noon; 10 of the 12 injected cocaine; antisocial personality disorder 58% against none in controls.

tasks.locator: Outcome › Mood Scores; Craving for Cocaine (p. 864); Table 2 and Figure 2 (p. 865)
tasks.extracted: Mood distress and Beck depression scores were higher in the cocaine group and fell over time more than in controls (Beck depression F = 13.949 for group, 10.670 for time, 8.526 for interaction; total mood distress 5.082, 9.359, 5.537); craving was highest on admission day and fell significantly over the 28 days (F = 17.270, df 10,110).

tasks.locator: Outcome › Self-reports of Sleep; Weight, Heart Rate, and Blood Pressure (p. 864, continued p. 866); Table 2 (p. 865)
tasks.extracted: Sleep reports did not differ from controls except more difficulty falling asleep in the cocaine group throughout (group F = 10.428); the other sleep measures improved over time in both groups; weight gain of 4.6 kg against 3.8 kg did not differ; heart rate rose 10.9 beats a minute in the cocaine group and fell 2.3 in controls.

tasks.locator: Comment, 2nd, 4th and 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors report that mood, craving and night waking improved gradually and were not cyclical or phasic in the first 4 weeks, unlike the earlier phase models, and suggest that the controlled setting, without cocaine or drug-taking cues, may explain the difference.

tasks.locator: Figure 1
tasks.extracted: In the plotted means, several Profile of Mood States scales in the cocaine group fall from day 1 to day 5, rise again around days 7 to 9 and then fall and stay low from about the second week; the paper reports no test of a phasic pattern (editors' reading of the figure; no values extracted).

tasks.locator: Comment, limitations paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Limitations named by the authors: a small all-male, mostly Black sample of mostly daily injectors; self-report; the experimental environment, which kept out the people and situations that could trigger conditioned responses; no standard last dose; only the first month; morning measures only.

tasks.locator: Figure and legend (p. 110); Phase 2: Withdrawal, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 111)
tasks.extracted: In outpatients, the crash was followed by one to five days of near-normal mood and sleep with little craving, then a fluctuating period of anhedonia, low energy, anxiety and irritability in which craving returned, lasting one to ten or more weeks (1 to 10 weeks in the figure); earlier attempts to stop had all failed within several days of this phase beginning.

tasks.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Methods › Study Selection (p. 2); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 5)
tasks.extracted: Nine studies with 246 young people were included from 9927 records and 167 full texts; eligibility required random assignment to stimulant conditions and actigraphy or polysomnography; studies were collected through March 2015.

tasks.locator: Methods › Data Extraction; Effect Size Calculation
tasks.extracted: Effect sizes compared baseline with medicated sleep, with placebo nights used where a study gave no baseline (4 studies), and a correlation of 0.5 was assumed when the needed statistics were missing.

tasks.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Sleep Latency, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Sleep latency, 7 samples (N = 171): g = 0.78 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.02), I² 67.30%; after trim-and-fill with 3 imputed studies, 0.54 (0.28 to 0.81).

tasks.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Sleep Efficiency
tasks.extracted: Sleep efficiency, 7 samples (N = 155): g = −0.39 (−0.69 to −0.08), I² 83.37%; after trim-and-fill with 1 imputed study, −0.32 (−0.63 to −0.01); the negative effect was smaller in studies with more days on medication (b = 0.05 per day).

tasks.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Total Sleep Time
tasks.extracted: Total sleep time, 7 samples (N = 223): g = −0.59 (−0.84 to −0.35), I² 82.67%, with no funnel-plot asymmetry and no significant moderators.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (read on the rendered, rotated page)
tasks.extracted: Single-study effects: sleep latency 0.44 to 1.15, all longer on medication; sleep efficiency −1.76 to 0.48, one study better on medication; total sleep −1.31 to −0.16, all shorter; mean ages 102 to 139.2 months.

tasks.locator: Limitations (p. 8); Conclusions and Funding (p. 9)
tasks.extracted: The authors note that publication bias was present for latency and efficiency, that the correction may underestimate effects and that moderator results rest on few studies; there was no external funding.

tasks.locator: Method › Sample, 2nd paragraph; Procedures (p. 514); Results › Patients, 1st paragraph (p. 515)
tasks.extracted: Children aged 6 to 14 on stable stimulant medicine with sleep-onset latency over 60 minutes on parents' diaries; those still above 60 minutes after sleep hygiene were randomized by the pharmacy in blocks of four to melatonin and placebo in a crossover with placebo washouts; of 23 eligible, 1 withdrew and 3 were discontinued for protocol violations, and 19 were analysed per protocol.

tasks.locator: Results › Melatonin Versus Placebo, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Diary sleep-onset latency was 46.4 minutes (SD 26.4) on melatonin and 62.1 (SD 26.6) on placebo, t(20) = −3.06, p < .01, effect size 0.6, with a significant period effect, t(20) = −2.20, and no carryover; actigraph latency was also shorter, t(18) = −4.54, p < .01; diary total sleep was 15.0 minutes longer, t(20) = 3.13.

tasks.locator: Results › Melatonin Versus Placebo, 3rd paragraph; Safety
tasks.extracted: Clinician-rated treatment response and ADHD ratings did not differ between melatonin and placebo; adverse events were mild or moderate except one severe migraine, the only study-related event was a rash from the actigraph band, and twenty per cent of all adverse events occurred during melatonin and 23% during placebo.

tasks.locator: Title page footnote (p. 512); Method › Medication and Statistical Analysis (p. 515); Disclosure (p. 518)
tasks.extracted: Sponsored as an investigator-initiated trial by Circa Dia BV, which manufactured the melatonin; the first author disclosed ties with Circa Dia and several makers of ADHD medicines; the study aimed to detect a 30-minute change with 25 children.

tasks.locator: Method › Sample, 2nd paragraph; Procedures › Sleep Hygiene
tasks.extracted: Inclusion required stimulant medicine at an unchanged dose and a mean sleep-onset latency over 60 minutes on 10 nights of parent diaries; sleep hygiene meant reviewing the diaries with parent and child, choosing a consistent bedtime and waking time, and stopping caffeine and naps.

tasks.locator: Results › Response to Sleep Hygiene, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Sleep-onset latency fell from 91.7 to 69.3 minutes on diaries (t(28) = 2.77, p = .01) and from 98.1 to 73.0 on actigraphy (t(21) = 2.92, p < .01), effect size 0.67; diary variability fell from 47.7 to 29.1 minutes; five children met the response criterion (under 1 hour); clinicians rated 21% much or very much improved, 21% minimally improved and 54% unchanged; ADHD ratings did not change.

tasks.locator: Abstract (p. 512); Results › Patients, 1st paragraph (p. 515)
tasks.extracted: The abstract gives twenty-seven children receiving sleep hygiene; the participant flow gives 33 consenting, five withdrawing and five responding to sleep hygiene, leaving 23 eligible for randomization; this phase had no control group.
